question: 1215: Fourth Lateran Council
answer: Dealt with the issue of transubstantiation and made the requirement for all Catholics to make at least one confession a year. Jews and Muslims living in Christin territories should also wear special dress.

question: 1262: Venice establishes a ‘national debt’
answer: Did this because they mainly traded by sea, which required the development and maintenance of a large navy, which was very expensive and carried high levels of risk for the state. The national debt allowed the government to tap into the resources of individual citizens (risk spread in case of failure).

question: 1414: Council of Constance
answer: Convened between 1414 and 1418, tasked with healing the Great Schism in the Catholic Church. It forced the resignation of three antipopes, and elected a new pope. Also reacted against reforms proposed by Jas Hus.

question: 1420: Treaty of troyes
answer: An important milestone of the Hundred Years’ War, this treaty was an agreement that Henry V of England would succeed to the French throne upon the death of Charles VI of France. Attempt to secure an end to the dynastic struggles between England and France. Charles VI agreed to marry his daughter to Henry V.

question: 1453: Ottoman conquest of constantinople
answer: Led by Sultan Mehmed II, deployed skillful use of archery. The fall of the city meant that the approached to central Europe lay open to invasion and Ottoman armies eventually reached the walls of Vienna.

question: 1454: Gutenberg Bible Printed in Mainz
answer: Using movable type at a speed not seen before. Proved that printed material could have widespread appeal and helped herald a revolution in how information and ideas were transmitted.

question: 1476: William Caxton Sets up first Printing Press in England
answer: Brought the knowledge he gained from Gutenberg back to England. Had a significant influence on the English language, as printed an widely disseminated material helped the process of standardizing the English language.

question: 1479: Gentile Bellini sent to paint Ottoman sultan Mehemed II
answer: Sultan Mehemed II was eager to have greater cultural contact with Italy, Bellini was sent to paint his portrait in an effort to secure diplomatic capital. Helped spread information about and generate interest in the Ottoman empire at a time when it was seen as foreign and extremely hostile.

question: 1485: Henry Tudor defeats Richard II of England at Bosworth field
answer: Final major battle of the War of the Roses. Richard had gained the English throne after the death of his older brother Edward IV and his nephews. Supporters of the House of Lancaster rallied behind Henry Tudor. Richard was killed in combat (his army had more people but they were bad at fighting.)

question: 1494: Treaty of Tordesillas
answer: Commercial and political agreement between the kingdoms of Aragon and Castile and Portugal. The Treaty formalized the details of a papal bull issued the year before that had given control of the Americas to Aragon and Castile and Africa and India to Portugal. (this was then changed to longitudes)

question: 1495: charles VIII enters Naples
answer: An event of the Italian Wars. King Charles VIII of France had been promised the throne of the Kingdom of Naples by Pope Innocent VIII to help the latter in his power struggles on the Italian peninsula. Charles led an army into Italy, deposed the king and was crowned.

question: 1499: French Conquest of Milan
answer: By the end of the fifteenth century, Milan’s rulers paid Swiss mercenaries to protect the city. As a part of the Italian Wars, the French were able to defeat these forces and capture the city in 1499. Milan changed hands several times before being acquired by the Spanish Habsburgs in 1525.

question: 1508: League of Cambrai
answer: Worried by the potential long-term problems that a strong Venice could pose. Pope Julius II organized a collation including the Holy Roman Empire, France, Aragon, and many of the Italian city-states. This phase is often referred to as the ‘War of the League of Cambrai’ and continued until 1516. Whilst Venice was dealt short-term set-backs, they were not defeated in the long-term.

question: 1509: Battle of Agnadello
answer: Major battle of the Italian Wars between France and Venice. The French forces under command of King Louis XII were able to defeat two of Venice’s most experienced generals. Forced to retreat, Venice left its possessions in Lombardy undefended and lost much of the territory and influence.

question: 1515: France Regains Control of Milan
answer: Originally conquered by France in 1499, the city had changed hand several times since then. After their expulsion from Lombardy in 1512, the French regrouped and resupplied before capturing the city. Would lose it again but important victory for King Francis I.

question: 1516: Jewish Ghetto Established in Venice
answer: Named after a local foundry and surrounded by walls, similar ‘ghettos’ emerged in other cities. Jews were forced to live within these areas and confined there at night.

question: 1517: Luther’s Ninety-Five Theses
answer: Martin Luther’s denunciation of the sale of indulgences by the Catholic Church. Luther saw this practice as being one of the worst in a Church riddled by worldliness and corruption. Luther hoped to prompt reforms that would re-focus the Church on spiritual concerns. Touchstone of fierce debate.

question: 1521: Charled V Issues Edict of Worms
answer: Landmark movement in the development of the reformation, the Edict of Worms was issued by the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V at the Diet held there in 1521. Pope Leo X had excommunicated Martin Luther a few months earlier and ordered secular authorities to put him under the ban. Forbade Catholics from aiding or assisting him on pain of eternal damnation.

question: 1525: Battle of Pavia
answer: Major engagement of the Italian Wars. Fought between French forces under the command of King Francis I and Spanish/Holy Roman Empire forces, the battle was a crushing defeat for France. Francis was taken prisoner and French noble leadership and troops suffered massive losses. The French were forced to retreat across the Alps leaving Milan open to be re-taken by Emperor Charles V. This alarmed many and led to the establishment of the League of Cognac to help contain Spanish ambitions.

question: 1526: League of Cognac
answer: An attempt to contain Charles V’s forces after his decisive defeat of French forces at the Battle of Pavia. Brokered by Pope Clement VII, the League drew together the forces of France, Venice and various Italian city-states. Charles and his forces continued their successes and were able to defeat their adversaries, leading to the fall and sack of Rome in 1527. The League disintegrated in the face of defeats.

question: 1527: Sack of Rome
answer: When Charles’ army reached Rome in the spring of 1527 they laid siege (but morale was low). Eventually, they defeated Rome’s defenders and looted the city. Many were killed and much damage was done. Clement VII was captured by Charles’ troops, but the event embarrassed the Emperor. It also caused Clement in future to steer a political course that did not antagonize Charles.

question: 1529: Colloquy of Marburg
answer: Swiss theologian Huldrych Zwingli was developing a form of Protestantism that differed from Luther’s thinking. Protestant reformers attempted to bring Luther and Zwingli together to resolve their differences. It was the only time Luther and Zwingli met whilst the two were able to agree on many issues, they were not able to reach an agreement on the Eucharist. The result was 2 different denominations.

question: 1529: Ottoman Forces Lay Siege to Vienna
answer: By the early sixteenth century Ottoman armies had moved through Hungary and they reached Vienna by 1529. This caused panic in Christian Europe as it was felt that should Vienna be captured then the rest of the continent would fall to the Ottomans (led by Sultan Suleiman I). They were resisted by Imperial forces and troops of Bohemia and Spain. Vienna was besieged by the Ottoman forces in the fall of 1529 but poor weather and vulnerable supply lines forced them to withdraw. Represented the maximum extent of their expansion into Europe.

question: 1529: Protestation of Speyer
answer: In a reaction to the Edict of Worms (1521), six Protestant princes of the Holy Roman Empire and 14 free cities petitioned the Diet, during its meeting at Speyer, to lift the ban on Martin Luther and argued for the unhindered spreading of Luther’s works and teachings. Gave name to Protestants. Highlighted growing acceptance of the Reformation’s criticism of the Roman Catholic Church.

question: 1530: Ausburg Confession
answer: Luther’s followers made a formal submission to the Imperial Diet at Ausburg in an attempt to justify their position. It contained 21 articles considered fundamental to the Christian faith and seven condemning Catholic errors. Following its rejection by Charles V, the religious division within the Empire became more formalized. Fundamental statement of Lutheran beliefs and was incorporated into the Formula of Concord (1580).

question: 1534: Anabaptist takeover of Münster
answer: Several branches of this radical Protestant group had emerged from the 1520s. Their followers sought to return to a primitive version of Christianity and practiced adult baptism. They attempted to create a new Jerusalem in preparation for the second coming of Christ. Retaken in the summer of 1535, the rebellion’s leaders were tried and executed.

question: 1535: Charles V Captures Tunis
answer: Then under control of the Ottoman empire, the campaign was successful and Spanish/Holy Roman Empire troops sacked the city. It also became apparent from evidence found in the city that the French had been providing arms to Ottoman forces. The defeat advanced negotiations between the Ottoman empire and France who eventually agreed to a commercial treaty.

question: 1541: Ottomans Retain Algiers
answer: Holy Roman Emperor Charles V organised a campaign to take Algiers, another strategically important north-African territory under Ottoman control. This attempt was a disaster with considerable loss, nearly cost Charles his life and ended his practical ambitions to gain further territory in north Africa. The victory also stabilized Ottoman forces in the region.

question: 1545: Council of Trent
answer: Summoned by Pope Paul III to deal with the issues exposed by the Reformation. The council addressed perceived abuses, such as the sale of indulgences, but also re-affirmed key pillars of Catholic doctrine, the primacy of the Pope and the spiritual authority of the Church. This strengthened episcopal control.

question: 1547: Battle of Mühlberg
answer: Fought in Saxony between Imperial troops and the armies of the League of Schmalkalden. The Emperor captured the leading Protestant commanders. It ended the league, but Charles was unable to stem the rise of Protestantism or bring the members back into the fold of the Catholic Church. Led to the interim and eventual the peace of Ausburg.

question: 1548: Interim of Ausburg
answer: Decree of the Holy Roman Empire’s Imperial Diet dealing with Emperor Charles V’s victory over the League of Schmalkalden. It attempted to force Protestants back into the Catholic Church, the Interim actually started to legally enshrine elements of Protestantism and stands as an important milestone on the road to the legitimisation of Protestantism as a valid stand of Christianity.

question: 1552: France captures Metz
answer: French King Henry II pursued the aggressive military policy against Charles V. This involved capturing the independent cities of Metz, Toul and Verdun (bordered strategic positions on to borders of the French kingdom). By capturing them, an event secured at the Battle of Renty in 1554, Henry was able to further secure his kingdom and make it more difficult for Charles’ forces to mount campaigns into France.

question: 1555: Religious Peace of Ausburg
answer: A treaty that formally ended the War of the League of Schmalkalden. Ferdinand I became Holy Roman Emperor. The Peace recognised Lutheranism as the sole Protestant confession allowed within the Empire. The failure to accept Calvinists and other non-Lutheran Protestants led to conflicts in the Empire and ultimately contributed to the outbreak of the Thirty Years War.

question: 1559: Genevan Academy founded
answer: Became an important model of clerical education and a source of countless preachers helping to spread Calvinist teaching across Europe.

question: 1559: Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis
answer: Treaty that officially ended the Italian Wars. The peace conference saw Henry II of France and Philip II of Spain agree to terms delineating spheres of influence and areas of control for both countries in respect to the Italian states. Only Venice and Savoy retained any form of independence from foreign powers. The Peace was also notable for the death of the French King Henry II.

question: 1563: Academy of Art Founded in Florence
answer: Founded by Florantine ruler Cosimo I de’Medici. Served as a training centre and trade guild for active artists as well as a meeting place and social area for eminent artists. Its model had significant influence on other national art movements. Members included many significant artists active in Italy, including Michelangelo.

question: 1565: Ottoman Forces Fail to Capture Malta
answer: The Siege of Malta was a bloody and violent campaign. Malta was of strategic importance, held by Christian Knights since 1530 and was a major political, cultural and economic crossroad in the central Mediterranean. They Knights Hospitaller and Maltese citizens, aided eventually by Spanish and Sicilian forces, held out for nearly 4 months before finally forcing the Ottomans to retreat.

question: 1569: Union of Lubin
answer: Established the Commonwealth of Poland-Lithuania.

question: 1571: Battle of Lepanto
answer: A naval battle fought in the Gulf of Corinth (Greece) between the Holy League and the Ottoman fleet. Overall, Ottoman forces had maintained the upper hand, successfully expelling the Venetians from Cyprus earlier in the year and restricting trade generally. Nevertheless, the Holy League secured victory at Lepanto. First naval defeat for the Ottomans in nearly a century.

question: 1588: Spanish Naval Armada Defeated by the English
answer: Prior to the accession of Elizabeth I to the English throne, Philip II of Spain had been co-monarch. As a devout catholic, Philip considered Elizabeth a heretic and thus an illegitimate monarch. In order to regain the English throne, Philip organised a vast invasion fleet called the Armada. Philip and the Catholic world were confident of an easy victory. Poor planning, terrible weather and stiff English resistance caused the Armada to be a total failure. Other military action on the part of the English also prevented the Spanish from coordinating their forces and resulted in the loss of nearly a third of the Spanish ships. Boosted Elizabeth’s reputation.

question: 1598: Edict of Nantes Issued by Henry VI
answer: French King Henry IV had been born Protestant but converted to Catholicism in 1593, following the St Bartholomew’s Day Massacre. He sought to repair damage done to French society by the Wars of religion. The Edict extended official tolerance and political protection of Protestants in France. Protestants were granted many civil rights and were allowed to worship. The edict was revoked by King Louis XIV in 1685.

question: 1605: Gunpowder Plot in England
answer: Attempt to assassinate King James I at the opening of Parliament on 5 November 1605, by detonating a massive explosion in a cellar under the House of Lords. Catholic hopes for toleration had been high upon James’s accession in 1603, when these hopes were disappointed action was planned. Associated with Guy Fawkes, the leader was Robert Catesby. After the plot was discovered, Catesby was killed resisting arrest. Some historians have claimed the plot was set up by chief minister Robert Cecil to discredit Catholics, but this is improbable. Consequences for the English Catholic community was severe  ‘Anti-popery’

question: 1609: Amsterdam Bank Founded
answer: An early attempt to centralize and guarantee banking activities. Operated under the auspices of the city in order to regulate the quality of the money circulating. This provided greater certainty to both merchants and consumers that their transactions were fair.

question: 1619: Synod of Dordrecht
answer: Controversy had occurred because of the rise of Arminianism (a school of thought that differed from mainstream Protestantism on issues relating to how a believer achieves salvation). Arminianism was eventually condemned by the Synod but the meeting did help to moderate more conservative elements within the Dutch ecclesiastical establishment. The Synod is also notable for its decision to invite members of Reformed churches from outside the Netherlands to participate in its proceedings.

question: 1620: Battle of the White Mountain
answer: Early battle in the Thirty Years’ War, saw the decisive defeat of the forces of Frederick the ‘winter king’ who had been elected king of Bohemia in 1619. The defeat ended the Bohemian Uprising and saw Frederick of Styria crowned King of Bohemia. Did little to prevent the development of a larger conflict.

question: 1624: Parlement of Paris Requires Automatic Appeal of Cases from Lower courts
answer: The Parlement in Paris was given the power to examine all judgements passed by lower courts. This both increased the power of that body and helped to standardise legal practices across much of France. Standardisation meant that regional practices or local interpretations of laws became harder to sustain.

question: 1626: Battle of Lutter
answer: Crushing defeat of Danish forces by an Imperial army led by Johan Tzerclaes, Count of Tilly. Effectively ended Danish participation in the Thirty Years’ War.

question: 1631: Battle of Breitenfeld
answer: A major defeat of Imperial forces under the Count of Tilly, the Battle saw Swedish and Saxon forces destroy a large army. Led by Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus, the Protestant army routed its Catholic opponents giving the first Protestant victory over Catholic forces in the Thirty Years’ War. Although the conflict continued for some time, Breitenfeld showed that Emperor Ferdinand II’s policies, such as the 1629 edict of Restitution would not be implemented unopposed. Indeed, it has been argued that Protestant victory at Breitenfeld helped save the Protestant cause. The victory also proved that Gustavus Adolphus’s tactics were revolutionary and successful and cemented Sweden’s reputation as a European power until Swedish forces were defeated decisively at the Battle of Nördlingen in 1634.

question: 1632: Battle of Lüzten
answer: Although Swedish troops soundly defeated forces of the Holy Roman Empire and Catholic league at this battle, Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus was killed at the height of battle. For the protestant cause this was a significant setback, since Gustavus had become a leader due to his dynamic personality.

question: 1633: Galileo’s trial in rome
answer: Caught up in the politics of the Papal court, Galileo was declared a heretic and brought to a trial before the Roman Inquisition. Forced to choose between his work and the threat of excommunication from the Church, Galileo reluctantly recanted and was heavily sanctioned by the Church. He lived the rest of his life in house arrest.

question: 1634: Battle of Nördlingen
answer: Imperial forces were able to regain the initiative with their decisive defeat of combined Swedish and Protestant forces at this battle. Joining an imperial army with Spanish forces marching north from Italy, Ferdinand of Hungary presented a threat to Protestant territories in southern Germany that the latter could not ignore.

question: 1635: peace of prague
answer: Despite important foreign involvement, until the mid-1630s the Thirty Years’ War had been largely a civil war within the HRE. Neither side had been able to make definitive gains. Finally, exhausted by 1635, both major groups within the Empire agreed to a peace treaty ending the civil war. The treaty saw the Edict of Restitution rescinded, the forbidding of intra-Empire alliances, the establishment of an Imperial army and the disbandment of territorial armies, and a general amnesty for all princes and individuals who had fought against the Emperor. Although this peace did not end all hostilities of solve the root problems, it was a major steppingstone to the peace of Westphalia.

question: 1640: Parlement of Paris forbids prosecutions for witchcraft within its jurisdiction
answer: Because it automatically reviewed the judgements of lower courts within its area of oversight, the Paris parlement examined all witchcraft convictions. With the local panic removed, the number of prosecutions upheld began to drop significantly after about 1620. By the end of the 1630s, the quality and effectiveness of witchcraft prosecutions had been brought into considerable question and the value of such trials became highly suspect. Therefore, in 1640, the parlement in Paris refused to allow any prosecutions of witchcraft. It should be noted that this did not necessarily mean that suspected witches stopped being tried in other courts but is a general indication of the lessening of the panic over witchcraft in western Europe.

question: 1643: Battle of Rocroi
answer: A major engagement in the phase of the Thirty Years’ War that saw France and Spain in direct conflict. Rocroi was a fortified town with great strategic value to Spanish forces defending the Spanish Netherlands. The French soundly defeated the Spanish forces.

question: 1647: Masaniello leads ani-spanish revolt in naples
answer: Naples was a Spanish possession in the 17th century, the conflict was deeply unpopular due to taxation and riots began, where Tommaso Aniello (Masaniello) stepped forward and became the populist leader of a full-scale revolt. Ultimately he was not able to maintain balance, in part due to his increasingly erratic behaviour. He was eventually murdered but Spanish control over the city remained shaky.

question: 1648: Peace of münster
answer: Dutch importance in the European context had reached such a level that the Republic was invited to participate in the negotiations for the Peace of Westphalia despite not being a formally recognised state. Representatives of the two sides met in the city of Münster where the majority of the negotiations took place. Ultimately, the Spanish were willing to recognise the Dutch Republic as a sovereign state, which led to similar acceptance across Europe.

question: 1648: Peace of Westphalia
answer: The Thirty Years’ War was a protracted international conflict that started as a religious struggle but spread into a larger war involving all major European states. The Peace of Westphalia, signed in 1648, ended that conflict. It also represented a major realignment of European boundaries by recognising the virtual sovereignty of the German states within the Holy Roman Empire, establishing the independence of the Dutch Republic, exempting the Swiss Confederation from imperial control, and seeing strategically important territories given to Sweden, France, and Brandenburg. Protestants, including Lutherans as well as Calvinists, made further gains in areas of political recognition and official tolerance. The Peace is also credited with establishing the modern European state system and diplomatic practices still in use today.

question: 1648: Uprising in moscow against taxation
answer: Russian finances were decimated. Young tsar, Alexis I and his chief advisor Boris Morozov attempted to reform taxation and thus grow state revenues and imposed a universal salt tax. Because non-nobles paid the majority of taxes, this led to considerable economic distress for the most vulnerable members of Russian society. The Rebellion was put down and increased Alexis’ desire to press through with legal and military reforms that further entrenched state power in Russian society.

question: 1659: Peace of the Pyrenees
answer: The Treaty of Westphalia ended the general conflict of the Thirty Years’ War, but France and Spain had fought for another 11 years. France was in a strong bargaining position. Territorial gains through the Treaty of Westphalia had allowed France to cut the land link between Austria and the Spanish Netherlands and French armies had proven a match for Spanish forces in battle. Long-lasting peace was not achieved and the two states were at war again by 1668.

question: 1660: Royal society founded in london
answer: Served as a quasi-governmental body that was able to help develop the sciences.

question: 1660: Treaty of copenhagen
answer: Between 1655 and 1660, states in northern Europe and the Baltic area were embroiled in what was known as the Second Northern War. A coalition led by Sweden attempted to consolidate Swedish territorial gains in eastern Europe. Poland-Lithuania, Demark-Norway, the Habsburgs, and others resisted them. There were many reversals but ultimately Sweden found itself on the defensive. The borders between the major Scandinavian states were established.

question: 1666: Académie des sciences founded in paris
answer: Like the other one, but French and much more aligned to the royal government.

question: 1666: Great fire of London
answer: The fire, aside from highlighting the dangers of living in closely built cities constructed mainly of wood, also destroyed one of the most populous cities in Europe. It was a tense time politically in England, coming so soon after the restoration of the monarchy following the Commonwealth, but ultimately the fire did not lead to any major social upheavals. London was rebuilt, largely in a similar layout to the destroyed street plan

question: 1685: Edict of nantes revoked by louis XIV
answer: King Henry IV of France had issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, thereby providing the Huguenots with some degree of religious toleration and state protection. Growing pressure and lobbying convinced King Louis XIV to revoke the edict, as well as call for the destruction of Protestant churches and forces conversion of non-Catholics. This damaged Louis’ international prestige and deprived France of the skills and resources of an important minority as Huguenots took their money and skills and fled to neighbouring Protestant states.

question: 1698: Whitehall palace in Westminister is destroyed by fire
answer: With its destruction and no successful efforts to rebuild a similar structure on the site, royal focus moved away from London and to other palaces, such as the complex at Kensington.

question: 1755: Lisbon Earthquake
answer: A major earthquake, potentially one of the most powerful in recorded history, devastated the Portuguese capital on the morning of 1 November 1755. Coinciding with Enlightenment efforts to understand the natural world through science and observation, the Lisbon earthquake also prompted serious study of seismology.

question: 1789: Storming of the bastille
answer: Built in 1730 and used as a prison for political dissidents, the Bastille fortress had become an emblem of the French monarchy and its oppression and shortcomings. On 14 July 1789, an anti-government mob successfully stormed the fortress, killing its governor and freeing the handful of prisoners held. This was the first act of open rebellion and is considered the start of the French Revolution.

question: 1793: Opening of the Louvre palace as a public art gallery
answer: Following the overthrow of the French monarchy during the early stages of the French Revolution, attention turned towards how to utilize the many buildings and resources formerly owned by the monarchy. These included a vast collection of art, accumulated over many years. In thinking inspired by the Enlightenment, it was decided to turn the Louvre, a large and ornate palace in central Paris, into a gallery accessible to the public.

question: 1797: France conquers venice
answer: By the eighteenth century, however, strong competition from other European states and a resurgent Ottoman Empire had reduced Venice’s reach and influence. Also, Venice was structurally and financially unable to defend itself against the new military threats presented by the French Revolution and the rise of Napoleon Bonaparte. Napoleon’s interest in northern Italy was primarily due to his desire to defeat Austrian forces and take important territories north of Venice. Although neutral, Venice’s position was too strategic to be ignored and both France and Austria were willing to divide Venetian territory in order to best further their own ambitions. Venice’s thousand-year position as an independent European state ended on 18 October 1797 with the signing of the Treaty of Campo Formio.
